paper_title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two alternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator's intermediate features to estimate each token's remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing preserves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ~1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5x faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ~2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35x faster at 24.5 fps.

sections.title: Speculative Forcing for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion models have enabled high-quality image and video generation, with recent video models achieving realistic appearance, natural motion, and faithful prompt following (Team Wan et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; NVIDIA et al., 2026; Team Seedance et al., 2026). Autoregressive (AR) video generators extend these capabilities to streaming generation (Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025) and interactive world models (Team et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026; AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026). Within video, however, different regions may require different amounts of refinement. Some may readily reproduce familiar content from the history, while others must form newly appearing structures or resolve fine details. This raises fundamental question: Does every token need to be denoised until the final step? We study this question in distilled few-step AR video generators, whose intermediate predictions can already serve as plausible video outputs. Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025) uses intermediate clean estimates as outputs for distribution-matching training (Yin et al., 2024b;a), making them natural candidates for early commitment. We observe that many tokens already approximate the generators own full-step output in the initial steps, while others continue changing until the last step (Figure 2). These differences often follow intuitive patterns. Regions that reproduce previously observed content can settle early, while nearby regions continue refining appearance or motion. Similar variation arises in world models as actions change the observed content. These observations motivate simple principle: stop denoising tokens once they have converged, and spend the remaining computation only where refinement is still needed. We introduce Speculative Forcing, framework that predicts when each tokens estimate has sufficiently converged, allowing individual tokens to be accepted at different steps (Figure 1). Each intermediate clean estimate serves as draft of the generators full-step output. verifier determines whether to accept the draft or continue refining it. Once accepted, the estimate is fixed as the tokens output and receives no further denoising updates, while retaining its cached keys and values as context for the remaining tokens. This requires predicting whether tokens current draft is already close to its full-step output without running the remaining denoising steps. We address this challenge with two verifiers. Because drafts are clean latent estimates, similarity to previously generated content and changes between consecutive estimates of the same token provide evidence of convergence without additional training. Our training-free verifier uses similarity to clean history or reference content at the first step and stability between consecutive drafts at later steps. We also introduce learned verifier for demanding settings such as world models, leveraging contextual cues encoded in the pretrained generators intermediate features. shallow head trained with the generator frozen predicts each tokens gap to the full-step output, showing that the intermediate features contain cues about how much its predictions will change with further denoising. Both verifiers support token-wise acceptance without modifying the generators weights. We evaluate Speculative Forcing on LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a) and the world model LingbotWorld 2.0 (Gao et al., 2026). On both short and long videos, our method maintains the quality of the four-step generator with approximately 1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5 faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On controllable world model rollouts, harder setting where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with approximately 2.5 denoising steps per token, running 1.35 faster at 24.5 fps.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Autoregressive Video Generation. Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate successive frames or chunks conditioned on preceding content (ai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; 2024a). Distribution matching distillation (Yin et al., 2024b;a) enables few-step generation by aligning the students output distribution with target distribution represented by pretrained teacher. CausVid applies distribution matching to distill bidirectional teacher into causal generator (Yin et al., 2025), while Self Forcing trains on autoregressive rollouts conditioned on the generators own outputs (Huang et al., 2025). Causal Forcing revisits this distillation for real-time interactive generation (Zhu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). LongLive, Rolling Forcing, and Self-Forcing++ extend few-step generation to long streaming videos (Yang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b; Cui et al., 2025).

sections.content: Figure 2: Token-wise convergence during denoising. We visualize latent differences between each chunks k-step prediction and the baseline four-step output. (a) In video generation, background and object regions that remain similar to history tend to converge early, while other regions continue to change. (b) In world generation, previously observed regions often converge early, whereas newly revealed regions tend to require further denoising. The same few-step AR recipe underlies real-time interactive world models, which additionally condition generation on actions or camera trajectories (Team et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Seo et al., 2026; AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026). These generators produce clean latent estimate at every denoising step, not only the last, so an intermediate estimate can serve as final output. Adaptive Denoising. Caching methods accelerate diffusion by reusing intermediate computation across denoising steps (Ma et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024b; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a), including reuse selected per token (Zou et al., 2025) and, in AR video generation, per chunk or by local motion (Ma et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Spatially adaptive samplers redistribute computation within the schedule, with RAS recomputing only the regions the model attends to (Liu et al., 2026) and HSA evaluating each token at different number of steps along the same noise schedule (Chu & Patel, 2026). In both cases every token is carried to the end of the schedule, so no token is ever declared finished, and the error left by the computation that was skipped has to be kept bounded by periodic full updates. Substituting previous output also weakens as the schedule shortens, since distilled samplers leave fewer steps over which one output can stand in for the next (Zou et al., 2026). In Self Forcing-style generators, DSA and Surprise Forcing select denoising depth for an entire frame or chunk, assigning the same number of steps to settled and unsettled regions (Le et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Speculative Forcing instead treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts that can be committed at different steps according to token-wise convergence (Figure 2). It draws on draft verification in speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024), without adopting its exact acceptance rule. Committed tokens receive no further denoising updates, while their cached keys and values remain as context for the remaining tokens.

sections.content: Speculative Forcing allows individual tokens to stop denoising at different steps. Accepted drafts are fixed as output, while their cached keys and values provide context for tokens that continue denoising (Section 3.2). To determine when to accept each draft, we introduce two verifiers that predict convergence from latent estimates or the generators intermediate features (Section 3.3). 3.1 PRELIMINARIES Autoregressive video diffusion. Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate video as sequence of latent chunks {c1, c2, . . . }, each containing one or more consecutive frames. The joint distribution is factorized as p(c1, c2, . . . ) = (cid:81) p(ct c<t), where each conditional distribution is modeled through diffusion process. At inference, the model generates each chunk by progressively denoising Gaussian noise conditioned on previously generated chunks. We consider generators that use clean history Ht = c<t as conditioning and cache its keys and values to avoid recomputing history features during subsequent generation.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENT
sections.content: We evaluate Speculative Forcing on autoregressive video generation and world modeling. We compare generation quality and inference speed against uniform-step sampling, and examine whether preserving settled predictions while selectively refining the remaining tokens reduces error drift during autoregressive rollouts. We further analyze the verification tolerance, token selection, and the granularity of step allocation. 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS Experimental setups. We apply our method to LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a) (1.3B) and the CausalFast model of Lingbot-World 2.0 (Gao et al., 2026) (1.3B), both using four denoising steps. We keep both generators frozen and evaluate training-free and learned verifiers. For LongLive, we train the learned verifier on full-step rollouts from 1K VidProM (Wang & Yang, 2024) prompts following the generators original training rollout procedure. For Lingbot, we collect training rollouts from 1K initial images with scenes disjoint from evaluation, using the same random camera-trajectory sampling and rollout protocol as evaluation. Both use the same 3-layer 3D convolutional head with negligible overhead.ursH uses the head verifier, while OursTF uses the training-free verifier. The verification tolerance can be adjusted at inference without retraining. We set the learned verifiers tolerance to ϵ = 0.28 for short videos and use more conservative ϵ = 0.24 for long videos and world model rollouts. For each setting, we calibrate the training-free thresholds (τred, τstab) on held-out calibration data against the oracle convergence criterion relk(i) ϵ, using the same tolerance as the learned verifier. We compare against uniform sampling with one, two, three, and four denoising steps and report mean denoising steps and throughput on single NVIDIA H100. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A. Evaluation. For LongLive, we evaluate 5-second videos using the VBench prompts rewritten by Self Forcing (Huang et al., 2025), with five random seeds per prompt, and report all 16 VBench dimensions (Huang et al., 2023). We also generate 30-second videos with the same prompt set and evaluate all 16 dimensions using VBench-Long (Huang et al., 2024), following the protocol of LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a). We further evaluate Lingbot on 200 held-out navigation scenes to examine performance under substantial changes in visible content and pronounced intermediate distortions. Each scene provides an initial image, text prompt, and camera trajectory composed of five segments with randomly sampled camera actions and motion speeds. We generate 253 frames per scene and report VBench quality aggregate over six dimensions, excluding temporal flickering. We also report relative camera-pose error against the commanded ground-truth trajectory to assess whether accelerated sampling follows the camera path as faithfully as the four-step generator. For both long videos and world model rollouts, we additionally report the Drift metric of Reward Forcing (Lu et al., 2025), which measures temporal variation in imaging quality across video segments. All methods share the same conditioning inputs and sampling seeds. Metric definitions and benchmark construction are detailed in Appendix B. 4.2 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

Both our head and training-free verifiers preserve visual quality comparable to the four-step baseline without visibly increasing quality drift over the illustrated rollouts on our benchmark. 4.3 ABLATION STUDIES We examine how verification tolerance, verification signals, and acceptance granularity affect generation quality and efficiency. Figure 5 provides representative qualitative comparisons of the alternative policies. We further evaluate how accurately each verification signal predicts the oracle in Appendix C.1 and provide additional ablations on our head in Appendix C.2. Effect of verification tolerance. Table 4 shows how ϵ controls the quality-efficiency trade-off on Lingbot. Increasing ϵ reduces mean denoising steps, with ϵ = 0.20 and ϵ = 0.24 maintaining the four-step generators quality while achieving lower Drift. Larger tolerances accept insufficiently refined drafts and degrade quality, highlighting the need to balance early acceptance with further refinement. Effect of verification signals. We adapt two existing selection criteria to token-wise commitment in latent space. Inspired by MotionCache (Xu et al., 2026), we measure temporal differences between adjacent latent frames at the same spatial position. We also adapt RASs predicted-noise dispersion signal (Liu et al., 2026) to the channel variance of each predicted clean latent token. Thresholds are calibrated on held-out data to obtain comparable mean denoising steps. As shown in Table 5, both adapted signals yield lower quality than our learned verifier and uniform sampling at similar mean steps. Temporal differences, for example, can reflect both camera-induced changes and intermediate distortions, limiting their reliability as convergence signals (Figure 5). These results support directly predicting each drafts remaining convergence gap. Comparison with oracle verification. We additionally evaluate an oracle verifier that computes the full-step reference for each chunk using the same initial noise and conditioning, then uses the measured convergence gaps to determine token acceptance. We apply the same tolerance and spatiotemporal smoothing as the learned verifier. Our learned verifier achieves generation quality comparable to oracle verification without computing the full-step reference at inference  (Table 5)  .

Adaptive denoising has been explored at frame and chunk granularity (Le et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). To isolate commitment granularity, we use the same learned verifier but accept an entire chunk when its mean predicted convergence gap falls below threshold at each step. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced Speculative Forcing, framework that allocates denoising computation according to token-wise convergence in few-step autoregressive video generation. By treating intermediate clean estimates as drafts, it predicts which tokens can be accepted early and continues denoising only the remaining tokens. Training-free and learned verifiers enable these decisions without modifying the generators weights. Experiments on short and long videos and controllable world model rollouts demonstrate faster generation while maintaining quality, with comparable or lower quality variation and preserved camera-following accuracy in world modeling. These results show that shared denoising depth is not necessary for every token, supporting convergence-based acceptance as practical approach to efficient video generation.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: We retain the released backbone configurations except for the denoising policies evaluated in this work. For LongLive (Yang et al., 2025a), we use an attention sink of 3 latent frames, local attention window of 12 latent frames, and 3 latent frames per chunk. Short and long videos contain 81 and 477 frames, respectively. For Lingbot-World 2.0 (Gao et al., 2026), we use the 1.3B Causal-Fast model with an attention sink of 6 latent frames, local attention window of 18 latent frames, and 4 latent frames per chunk. Each benchmark video contains 253 frames. Lingbot-World 2.0 additionally receives per-frame camera trajectory encoded through Plucker embeddings derived from relative camera-to-world poses. We retain the original camera-conditioning pathway, including per-video translation normalization by the maximum translation magnitude. For the main results, the trainingfree thresholds (τred, τstab) are (0.497, 0.327) for 5-second LongLive videos, (0.357, 0.235) for 30-second LongLive videos, and (0.375, 0.300) for Lingbot-World 2.0. We retain the original denoising schedules so that early commitment operates on the intermediate clean estimates supervised during distribution-matching training. In our configurations, LongLive and Lingbot-World 2.0 share the shifted timesteps [1000.0, 937.5, 833.3, 625.0], obtained from 1000-step flow-matching schedule with shift of 5.0. token accepted at step undergoes exactly the first steps of this schedule. Uniform-step baselines use the same prefixes, allowing us to compare token-wise acceptance with shared exit step along the same trained denoising trajectory. The learned verifier reads hidden states from the generators final transformer block without an additional backbone forward. The head consists of layer normalization and three 3D convolutions with channel dimensions 1536 96 48 1. The first two convolutions use 3 3 3 kernels with GELU activations, and the last uses 111 kernel. The heads output is average-pooled over 2 2 2 token blocks and expanded back to the original grid using nearest-neighbor interpolation. The head has 4.11M parameters and is shared across denoising steps. We train only the head using the smooth-ℓ1 loss and Adam with learning rate of 103 and batch size 4. Within each chunk, accepted tokens retain the layer-wise keys and values computed at their acceptance step, while active tokens update theirs as denoising continues. The cache can therefore contain KV states from different denoising steps. Once the chunk is complete, the generator performs clean forward pass over the assembled output at timestep 0, refreshing the KV states of all tokens regardless of their acceptance steps. Subsequent chunks thus attend to history states computed from the completed clean output. We apply spatiotemporal smoothing to each verifiers score map before thresholding at every verification step. Spatial smoothing uses normalized 9 9 Gaussian kernel with standard deviation of 1.0 token and reflect padding, applied independently to each latent frame. Temporal smoothing then averages scores over the current and subsequent latent frames within the same chunk, using Gaussian weights with standard deviation of 1.0 latent frame. Only tokens that have not yet been accepted are forwarded through the generator at subsequent denoising steps. We reduce execution overhead through shared indexing and in-place KV updates. We also merge each chunks clean pass with the next chunks first denoising pass while preserving timestep conditioning, attention dependencies, and KV update order. All baselines use the same applicable execution optimizations for fair throughput comparisons.

sections.title: B EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: B.1 EVALUATION METRICS We follow VBench (Huang et al., 2023) for 5-second videos and VBench-Long (Huang et al., 2024) for 30-second videos for LongLive, reporting all 16 dimensions. For Lingbot-World 2.0, we aggregate six quality dimensions using VBenchs official normalization and weights, excluding temporal flickering because intended camera motion can produce frame-to-frame pixel changes. Following Reward Forcing (Lu et al., 2025), we measure Drift as the standard deviation of imaging-quality scores across non-overlapping 2-second segments, averaged over videos. We use VBenchs MUSIQ model and preprocessing, with 7 complete segments per Lingbot evaluation and 15 segments per 30-second LongLive evaluation. Lower Drift indicates more consistent imaging quality over time.

Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025) generates scene descriptions spanning diverse categories and visual styles, and Z-Image-Turbo (Image Team et al., 2026) generates the initial images at 1376 768. The image and video models receive the same scene prompt, combining environment, subject, and perspective descriptions. After fixing the benchmark, we construct the verifiers training set from separate scenes using the same pipeline, filtering potential overlap through text and image similarity. Each video contains 253 frames, with the 252 camera transitions divided into five consecutive control segments of lengths 50, 50, 50, 50, and 52. For each segment, we uniformly sample an action from forward, backward, strafe left, strafe right, yaw left, yaw right, and stop, excluding the preceding segments action. Across the benchmark, this produces 593 translation, 276 rotation, and 131 stationary segments. Translation speeds are sampled from U(0.2, 1.0), with the fastest translation segment in each video set to 1.0 to match the models per-video translation normalization. Yaw rates are sampled from U(0.6, 2.0) degrees per frame. We choose the lower bound based on preliminary tests in which smaller commands produced little visible rotation. Camera intrinsics follow the official adapter defaults and remain fixed across methods.

D DISCUSSIONS
sections.content: D.1 LIMITATIONS The achievable acceleration depends on both the underlying generator and the difficulty of the generation domain. If the backbone is sensitive to reducing denoising steps, fewer tokens can be accepted early without degrading generation quality, which limits the attainable speedup. Similarly, more challenging domains may require additional refinement across larger fraction of tokens. This is evident in world generation, where large viewpoint changes introduce stronger distortions than standard video generation and result in higher mean denoising steps, as shown in Table 3. Our method therefore does not guarantee the same acceleration across different generators or domains. D.2 OTHER DISCUSSIONS Mean Steps and Realized Speed-up. The clean forward pass used to refresh the KV cache adds one full pass per chunk. Assuming computation scales linearly with token evaluations, the ideal speed-up relative to the four-step generator is 5/(k + 1). Approaches that reuse noisy KV states, such as CausalRCM (Zheng et al., 2026), could avoid this pass and move the ideal speed-up toward 4/k. In practice, throughput does not scale proportionally with the mean denoising depth k. Each chunk continues until its last active token is accepted, incurring forward-pass overhead at every executed step even when few tokens remain active. This overhead therefore depends on maxi k(i) within each chunk rather than the average across tokens. Reducing this overhead would bring the realized speed-up closer to the ideal implied by the mean denoising depth. D.3 POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS Our experiments focus on general video generation and world modeling, but token-wise commitment may be particularly effective when much of the target content is already constrained by available conditions. In talking-head generation (Huang et al., 2026), for example, the background can remain largely unchanged while motion is concentrated around the face and upper body. In environment-grounded world models such as Seoul World Model (Seo et al., 2026) and World Observer (Choi et al., 2026), warped scene observations and reference images provide visual evidence for parts of the target view, while uncovered regions require new content to be generated. Dexterous World Models (Kim et al., 2025) provide static scene renderings along the camera trajectory and generate interaction-induced changes while preserving unaffected content.
